unit.title: Crypto basics
unit.description: Blockchain, Bitcoin, Ethereum, stablecoins, wallets and the EU's MiCA regulation

steps.title: A shared ledger
steps.body:
A **blockchain** is a record of transactions **shared by thousands of computers** (nodes) all over the world. Nobody controls it on their own.

Transactions are grouped into **blocks**. Each block carries a fingerprint (**hash**) of the previous one: that's how they're chained together.

steps.title: Why it can't be rewritten
steps.body:
If someone changes an old transaction, that block's fingerprint changes and every block after it breaks. On top of that, the other nodes have the correct copy and reject the fake one.

To sneak a change through you'd need to control most of the network: on a big network like Bitcoin, that's hugely expensive.

steps.title: What it is and what it isn't
steps.body: A blockchain is a way to record who owns what **without a middleman**. It doesn't make an asset worth more or turn it into a safe investment: cryptocurrencies are very volatile, no guarantee scheme covers them and **you can lose everything you invest**.
steps.key: Blockchain: a shared, chained record that nobody can rewrite on their own.
steps.tip: Using blockchain doesn't make something a good investment.

steps.title: The first cryptocurrency
steps.body:
**Bitcoin** was born in 2009, created by someone using the pseudonym **Satoshi Nakamoto**. It's digital money sent from person to person without banks, recorded on its blockchain.

Its headline rule: there will never be more than **21 million** bitcoins. That's why its fans call it «**digital gold**».

steps.title: The halving
steps.body:
New bitcoins are created as a reward for whoever adds blocks (the miners). Every **210,000 blocks**, about **4 years**, that reward is cut in half: that's the **halving**.

50 → 25 (2012) → 12.5 (2016) → 6.25 (2020) → **3.125** (2024). After the 2024 halving, 93.75 % of all bitcoins had already been issued.

steps.title: Scarce isn't the same as safe
steps.body: The scarcity is programmed in, but the price depends on how many people want to buy it: there are no profits or interest behind it. Bitcoin has fallen more than 70 % several times. It's a very volatile asset and **you can lose everything you invest**.
steps.key: Bitcoin: a maximum of 21 million, with new issuance halving roughly every 4 years.
steps.tip: Programmed scarcity doesn't mean a guaranteed price.

steps.title: A computing race
steps.body:
In Bitcoin, **miners** group transactions into a block and race to find a number that makes the block's fingerprint (hash) meet a condition. There are no shortcuts: you have to try a huge number of combinations every second.

The first to do it adds the block and collects the **reward** plus the **fees**. This is **proof of work**.

steps.title: Why it uses so much energy
steps.body:
That race burns through vast amounts of electricity on specialised machines. And that's exactly what protects the network: to rewrite history you'd have to outdo the work of all the other miners combined.

The **difficulty** adjusts every 2,016 blocks so that a block is found every **10 minutes** on average.

steps.title: The alternative: proof of stake
steps.body: Ethereum dropped mining in 2022 and moved to **proof of stake**: transactions are validated by people who lock up their coins as collateral. It uses over 99 % less energy. But the technology doesn't change the price risk: in crypto **you can lose everything you invest**.
steps.key: Proof of work: you earn the right to add blocks by spending energy on calculations.
steps.tip: The energy used in mining is the price of making the record impossible to rewrite.

steps.title: A world computer
steps.body:
**Ethereum** (2015) is a blockchain where, as well as sending money, you can run programs: **smart contracts**. Its currency is **ether (ETH)**.

A smart contract is an «if this happens, do that» that runs on its own, with no middleman.

steps.title: What's built on top
steps.body:
• **Tokens:** coins created by other projects on Ethereum, like many stablecoins.
• **DeFi:** lending and trading without a bank.
• **NFTs:** digital certificates of ownership.

Every transaction pays a fee in ETH called **gas**, which goes up when the network is congested.

steps.title: More possibilities, more risks
steps.body: Bitcoin does one thing (scarce money); Ethereum is a platform. More features also mean more ways to fail: a bug in a contract's code can let someone drain it, and there's nobody to complain to. ETH is very volatile and **you can lose everything you invest**.
steps.key: Ethereum adds to Bitcoin the ability to run programs: smart contracts.
steps.tip: In a smart contract, code is law… even when it has a bug.

steps.title: Crypto that doesn't want to move
steps.body:
A **stablecoin** is a token that tries to always be worth the same as a currency, usually **1 dollar** (or 1 euro). The most widely used are **USDT** (Tether) and **USDC** (Circle).

They're used to move between cryptos without going through a bank and to make payments.

steps.title: How they hold their value
steps.body:
• **Reserve-backed:** the issuer holds cash and short-term government debt for every token. Risk: the reserves failing. In March 2023, USDC fell to around 0.87 $ when a bank holding part of its reserves collapsed.
• **Algorithmic:** no real reserves, just a mechanism tied to another crypto. **TerraUSD (UST)** collapsed in **May 2022** and dragged LUNA almost to zero.

steps.title: What MiCA requires
steps.body: In the EU, the **MiCA** regulation requires stablecoin issuers to be authorised, hold sufficient, segregated **reserves** and let you **redeem** tokens at par. Even so, «stable» doesn't mean «guaranteed»: they're not covered by the deposit guarantee scheme and **you can lose what you invest**.
steps.key: A stablecoin is worth what its reserves are worth, plus trust in its issuer.
steps.tip: If a stablecoin pays you 20 % «with no risk», ask where that money comes from.

steps.title: What a wallet holds
steps.body:
Your crypto isn't «inside» your wallet: it's on the blockchain. The wallet holds the **keys**:

• **Address (public key):** like your IBAN; you can share it to receive funds.
• **Private key:** the one that signs transfers. Whoever has it controls the money.

The **seed phrase** (12 or 24 words) lets you recover all your keys.

steps.title: Your own custody or someone else's
steps.body:
• **Third-party custody:** you leave your crypto on an exchange, which holds the keys. Convenient, but if it goes bust or freezes your account, you're at its mercy (FTX, 2022).
• **Self-custody:** you hold the keys (software or hardware wallet). Nobody can freeze them… but if you lose your seed phrase, **nobody** can recover them.

steps.title: The golden rule
steps.body: Your seed phrase goes **on paper or metal, offline**, somewhere safe. Never in a photo, an email or the cloud. **No legitimate party will ever ask you for it**: not support, not the exchange, not «Hacienda» (the Spanish tax authority). If you give it to someone, they take everything and there's no going back.
steps.key: «Not your keys, not your coins»: whoever controls the keys controls the crypto.
steps.tip: Anyone asking for your seed phrase is robbing you.

steps.title: What an exchange is
steps.body:
An **exchange** is a platform where you buy and sell crypto with euros or other cryptos. It almost always **holds** your crypto for you.

Under the EU's **MiCA** regulation, crypto-asset service providers need **authorisation** to operate in the EU.

steps.title: What MiCA requires of them
steps.body:
• **Authorisation** from a national supervisor (in Spain, the CNMV), valid across the EU.
• **Keeping** clients' crypto separate from their own.
• **Capital**, governance and conflict-of-interest requirements.
• Clear information and a **complaints** procedure.

According to the CNMV, from **1 July 2026** only authorised providers can operate in Spain.

steps.title: What MiCA doesn't do
steps.body: MiCA doesn't stop prices falling or create a guarantee fund for your crypto. It reduces the risk of the platform misusing your money, but crypto is still very volatile and **you can lose everything you invest**. Before opening an account, look the platform up in the **CNMV** or **ESMA** registers.
steps.key: MiCA requires exchanges in the EU to be authorised, keep client assets separate and be transparent.
steps.tip: Check the platform in the official register, not on its own website.

u12l1-1.prompt: Put in order how a transaction is recorded on a blockchain.
options: It's grouped with others into a block
The block is added to the chain and everyone updates their copy
The nodes check you have the balance
You send the transaction to the network
u12l1-1.explanation: Check, group, chain and copy: that way nobody needs to trust a middleman.

u12l1-2.prompt: Who controls a public blockchain like Bitcoin's?
options: Nobody on their own: thousands of nodes share the record
u12l1-2.explanation: That's its key feature: the record is spread across many participants.

u12l1-3.prompt: Changing an old transaction on a big blockchain is easy if you have a good computer.
u12l1-3.explanation: You'd have to redo every block after it and outpace the rest of the network: a single computer can't.

u12l1-4.prompt: Each block stores the fingerprint, or ____, of the previous block.
u12l1-4.explanation: A hash is a digital fingerprint: change a single piece of data and it changes completely.

u12l1-5.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.
u12l1-5.explanation: These are the four basic pieces of any blockchain.

u12l1-6.prompt: A project using blockchain guarantees that it's a good investment.
u12l1-6.explanation: The technology says nothing about the asset's value: many blockchain-based cryptos have lost almost all their value.

u12l1-7.prompt: What does a public blockchain achieve? Select all.
options: Makes rewriting the past very hard
Stops the crypto's price from falling
A record with no central middleman
u12l1-7.explanation: A blockchain protects the record, not the price.

u12l1-8.prompt: Quick: if someone tampers with an old block…
options: The chain of fingerprints breaks and the network rejects it
u12l1-8.explanation: The hash changes and no longer fits with the next block.

u12l1-9.prompt: Pablo reads in an ad: «Token X, powered by blockchain technology: a 100 % safe investment». What does he think?
options: That blockchain guarantees nothing about value, and «100 % safe» is a red flag
That he has to invest now, before it goes up
If it uses blockchain, it's safe
u12l1-9.explanation: Using technical jargon to promise safety is a common scam tactic.
feedback: Good: in crypto you can lose everything you invest; no serious party promises total safety.
Being rushed is another classic red flag.
Blockchain records transactions; it doesn't protect you from the price or from the project being a fraud.

u12l1-10.prompt: Does a blockchain do this or not?
options: Give you your money back if you get the address wrong
Keep copies on thousands of nodes
u12l1-10.explanation: What's recorded can't be undone: neither can your mistakes.

u12l2-1.prompt: What's the maximum number of bitcoins that can ever exist?
u12l2-1.explanation: It's set in the protocol: issuance slows down with each halving.

u12l2-2.prompt: About every 4 years, Bitcoin's block reward is cut in half: that's the ____.

u12l2-3.prompt: Put Bitcoin's block reward in order over time.
u12l2-3.explanation: Each halving divides the reward by two: issuance slows until it reaches 21 million.

u12l2-4.prompt: After the 2024 halving, the reward is 3.125 BTC per block. What will it be after the next halving?

u12l2-5.prompt: Bitcoin adds a block every 10 minutes on average. How many blocks are produced per day?

u12l2-6.prompt: This is a chart of one of the big cryptocurrencies, in daily candlesticks. What did it do over the next 10 sessions?
u12l2-6.explanation: In crypto, a few weeks can bring double-digit moves in either direction: that's why people talk about extreme volatility.

u12l2-7.prompt: Because the number of bitcoins is capped, its price always goes up.
u12l2-7.explanation: The price depends on demand. Even with its capped supply, Bitcoin has fallen more than 70 % several times.

u12l2-8.prompt: Bitcoin was created by someone using the pseudonym Satoshi ____.
u12l2-8.explanation: Their real identity is still unknown. Vitalik Buterin is the co-founder of Ethereum.

options: Its supply is limited, but its price is very volatile and it's fallen more than 70 % several times
It can't fall because there are only 21 bitcoins
u12l2-9.explanation: Scarcity explains part of Bitcoin's appeal, not its stability.
feedback: That's it! Scarcity isn't stability: in crypto you can lose everything you invest.
Even gold has spent years losing value, and Bitcoin has fallen more than 70 % on several occasions.
It's 21 million at most, not 21, and its price does fall.
lines: Bitcoin is digital gold, so it can never fall much, right? 🪙

options: What others are willing to pay for it
u12l2-10.explanation: It doesn't generate profits or interest: its price depends on adoption and demand.

u12l3-1.prompt: Put in order how a Bitcoin block is mined.
options: Tries combinations until it hits a valid hash
The block is added and the miner collects the reward and fees
The network checks the block is correct
u12l3-1.explanation: Finding the solution costs a lot; checking it, very little: that asymmetry is the basis of proof of work.

u12l3-2.prompt: What do miners earn for adding a block?
options: New bitcoins and the transaction fees
A salary from the central bank
u12l3-2.explanation: With each halving the reward drops, so fees will matter more and more.

u12l3-3.prompt: Mining difficulty adjusts so that a block is found roughly every 10 minutes.
u12l3-3.explanation: If more miners join, the difficulty goes up; if they leave, it goes down.

u12l3-4.prompt: Bitcoin mining uses little energy because it's just software.
u12l3-4.explanation: It uses specialised machines running non-stop: their electricity consumption is huge.

u12l3-5.prompt: Match each concept to its meaning.
u12l3-5.explanation: Two ways of deciding who adds the next block: by spending energy or by putting coins at risk.
right: How hard it is to find a valid block
Validating by putting up coins as collateral
Validating by spending energy on calculations

u12l3-6.prompt: Ethereum gave up mining in 2022 and moved to proof of ____.
u12l3-6.explanation: Proof of stake: validation is done by those who lock up ETH as collateral.

u12l3-7.prompt: Difficulty adjusts every 2,016 blocks. At 10 minutes per block, roughly every how many days is that?

u12l3-8.prompt: Quick: what does proof of work protect?
options: Making it hugely expensive to rewrite the record
u12l3-8.explanation: Attacking the network would take more computing power than all the other miners combined.

u12l3-9.prompt: Laura reads: «Mine bitcoins from your phone with our app and earn €50 a day». What does she think?
options: That she'll install it just to try
That it's an easy way to make money
That it's almost certainly a con: a phone can't compete with professional mining
u12l3-9.explanation: When a promise doesn't fit how the technology works, be suspicious.
feedback: Installing apps like this can expose your data or your wallet.
Real mining needs specialised machines and lots of electricity: a phone can't compete.
Good: many «mining apps» are scams or use your phone for other purposes.

u12l3-10.prompt: What's true about proof of work? Select all.
options: It makes attacking the network very expensive
Miners compete to solve a calculation
It uses a lot of electricity
u12l3-10.explanation: Ethereum dropped it in 2022 and moved to proof of stake.

u12l4-1.prompt: Match each concept to its meaning.
u12l4-1.explanation: The basic vocabulary for understanding what goes on inside Ethereum.
right: Program that runs by itself on the blockchain

u12l4-2.prompt: Match each item to what defines it.
u12l4-2.explanation: Bitcoin and Ethereum are separate networks; stablecoins and NFTs are things built on top.
right: Token that tries to always be worth 1 dollar or 1 euro

u12l4-3.prompt: What does Ethereum add to what Bitcoin does?
options: Running programs (smart contracts) on the blockchain
u12l4-3.explanation: That's why tokens, DeFi and NFTs are built on Ethereum.

u12l4-4.prompt: Ethereum gas is a fixed fee that never changes.
u12l4-4.explanation: It goes up when the network is congested and down when demand is low.

u12l4-5.prompt: If a smart contract has a coding bug, someone can exploit it and drain its funds.
u12l4-5.explanation: It has happened many times, and on a blockchain there's no bank to complain to.

u12l4-6.prompt: Is it a common use of Ethereum?
options: Protecting your crypto like a deposit guarantee scheme
u12l4-6.explanation: Ethereum makes lots of things possible, but none of them guarantees returns or protects your money like a deposit.

u12l4-7.prompt: A website asks you to connect your Ethereum wallet and sign a contract to «claim free tokens». What do you do?
options: Sign with my main wallet to get more
Not sign anything I don't understand and check the project through its official channels
u12l4-7.explanation: With smart contracts, one signature can authorise moving your entire balance.
feedback: Signing a contract you don't understand can give permission to empty your wallet.
If it's a trap, you'll lose everything in that wallet.
Good: many scams use smart contract signatures to steal.

u12l4-8.prompt: Quick: what currency is Ethereum gas paid in?
u12l4-8.explanation: Every transaction on Ethereum pays its fee in ether.

u12l4-9.prompt: Programs that run by themselves on Ethereum are called ____ contracts.
u12l4-9.explanation: Smart contracts: they run when their conditions are met, with no middleman.

u12l4-10.prompt: Sending some tokens costs 0.0005 ETH in gas and ETH is worth €2,000. How much do you pay in fees?
u12l4-10.explanation: 0.0005 × 2,000 = €1. If the network gets congested, it can cost a lot more.

u12l5-1.prompt: What does a stablecoin try to do?
options: Always be worth the same as a currency, like 1 dollar
u12l5-1.explanation: Its goal is stability against a currency, not growth.

u12l5-2.prompt: Match each case or concept to its meaning.
u12l5-2.explanation: Two real episodes that show both risks: no reserves, and reserves in trouble.
right: Fell to around 0.87 $ when a bank collapsed
Swapping 1 token for 1 dollar or 1 euro
Cash and debt backing each token

u12l5-3.prompt: A stablecoin is covered by the deposit guarantee scheme, like a bank account.
u12l5-3.explanation: Spain's deposit guarantee scheme (FGD) covers bank deposits, not crypto-assets.

u12l5-4.prompt: An algorithmic stablecoin has no real reserves backing it.
u12l5-4.explanation: It relies on a mechanism involving another crypto; if confidence breaks, it can spiral down.

u12l5-5.prompt: May 2022. Bruno has his savings in UST because a platform pays him almost 20 % a year «for being stable». UST starts trading at 0.95 $. What do we learn from what happened?
options: That stablecoins always go back to 1 $
That it was a chance to buy more
That a sky-high «stable» return was hiding a huge risk
u12l5-5.explanation: A high return that's supposedly risk-free usually hides a risk you can't see.
feedback: Some recover; UST didn't. «Stable» is a goal, not a guarantee.
Within days UST sank far below 1 $ and never recovered: anyone who bought more lost it.
Exactly: UST lost its peg and LUNA fell almost to zero in days. Lots of people lost almost everything.

u12l5-6.prompt: What does MiCA require of stablecoin issuers in the EU? Select all.
u12l5-6.explanation: MiCA aims to make sure the token is backed and redeemable, not that it earns anything.

options: Held up by another cryptocurrency and an algorithm
Holds dollars and Treasury bills for every token
u12l5-7.explanation: Reserve-backed ones depend on the backing actually existing; algorithmic ones, on trust in the mechanism.

u12l5-8.prompt: «Stable» means it's impossible to lose money with a stablecoin.
u12l5-8.explanation: UST collapsed in 2022 and even USDC lost its peg for a few days in 2023.

u12l5-9.prompt: In March 2023, the stablecoin ____ fell to around 0.87 $ when a bank holding its reserves collapsed.
u12l5-9.explanation: It regained its peg within a few days, once access to those reserves was secured.

u12l5-10.prompt: What's the main risk of a reserve-backed stablecoin?
options: The reserves not existing, not being available or losing value
u12l5-10.explanation: That's why MiCA requires sufficient, segregated and auditable reserves.

u12l6-1.prompt: Put in order the steps to set up a self-custody wallet safely.
options: Generate it and write the seed phrase down on paper
Keep the paper somewhere safe and offline
Send a small test amount before moving more
Download the wallet from its official website
u12l6-1.explanation: A trusted source, an offline copy of the phrase and a small test before risking more.

u12l6-2.prompt: Select the messages that are scams.
options: I'll send you back double if you send 0.1 ETH to this address 😉
Your wallet has been compromised. Verify your 24 words at this link to protect it.
Saw your problem on the forum. Send me your seed phrase and I'll recover your funds.
Remember: never share your seed phrase with anyone.
New login from another device. If it wasn't you, check your account in the app.
u12l6-2.explanation: No legitimate party asks for your seed phrase, and «I'll send you back double» is a classic. Alerts that point you to your own app without asking for details are normal.

u12l6-3.prompt: What does your seed phrase let you recover?
options: All the keys and crypto in your wallet
u12l6-3.explanation: That's why whoever has it can take everything.

u12l6-4.prompt: Where is it safest to keep your seed phrase?
options: On paper or metal, somewhere safe and offline
In an email you send to yourself
In a photo on your phone
u12l6-4.explanation: Anything connected to the internet can be stolen or leaked.

u12l6-5.prompt: You can share your public address so people can send you crypto.
u12l6-5.explanation: It's like giving out your IBAN: it's for receiving, not withdrawing.

u12l6-6.prompt: If you lose the seed phrase for a self-custody wallet, support can recover it for you.
u12l6-6.explanation: Nobody can: that's the price of not depending on anyone.

u12l6-7.prompt: Self-custody or custody on an exchange?
options: If you lose your seed phrase, you lose everything
If the platform goes bust, you may lose access
u12l6-7.explanation: Each option swaps one risk for another: the platform's, or your own mistakes.

u12l6-8.prompt: Ana keeps her crypto in self-custody. Someone from «technical support» messages her on Telegram: there's a fault and she needs to validate her seed phrase on a form. What does she do?
options: Fills in the form quickly so she doesn't lose anything
Sends them only half the words
Ignores the message: no legitimate support team asks for your seed phrase
u12l6-8.explanation: Your seed phrase is never shared, with anyone, through any channel.
feedback: She's just handed over her money: with the seed phrase, the scammer empties the wallet in minutes.
No part of the phrase is ever shared, and whoever is asking will keep pushing until they get the rest.
Good: it's one of the most common scams in crypto.

u12l6-9.explanation: The private key signs transfers: whoever has it is in charge.

u12l6-10.prompt: Match each item to its function.
u12l6-10.explanation: Knowing what each piece does tells you which one you can share (only the address) and which never.
right: Storing keys on an offline device

u12l7-1.prompt: What does MiCA require of an exchange operating in the EU? Select all.
options: Keeping clients' crypto separate from its own
u12l7-1.explanation: MiCA regulates the platform, not the price of crypto.

u12l7-2.prompt: Where do you check whether an exchange is authorised? Select all.
u12l7-2.explanation: Only official registers count: anyone can put a fake badge on their website.

u12l7-3.prompt: According to the CNMV, from 1 July 2026, who can provide crypto-asset services in Spain?
u12l7-3.explanation: That day the transition period in Spain came to an end.

u12l7-4.prompt: MiCA creates a guarantee fund that pays you back if your crypto falls in price.
u12l7-4.explanation: There's no such fund: price falls are your risk.

u12l7-5.prompt: A MiCA authorisation granted in another EU country allows a provider to operate in Spain.
u12l7-5.explanation: It works like a European passport: one authorisation is valid across the EU.

u12l7-6.prompt: Marta finds an exchange with very low fees and a welcome bonus, but it doesn't appear in the CNMV or ESMA registers. What does she do?
options: Looks for an authorised provider, even if it charges a bit more
Deposits a little to try it out
Uses it: fees are what matter most
u12l7-6.explanation: Just like with a broker: first who supervises it, then how much it charges.
feedback: Good: first make sure it's safe and supervised; then that it's cheap.
With an unauthorised platform, even a small amount can be lost with nobody to complain to.
Without authorisation, nobody checks whether it keeps your crypto separate or how it uses it.

u12l7-7.prompt: Match each acronym to its meaning.
u12l7-7.explanation: The acronyms you'll see in any warning about crypto platforms in Europe.

u12l7-8.prompt: Quick: what's the first thing you check about an exchange?
options: That it gives you a welcome bonus
That it has lots of cryptos to choose from
u12l7-8.explanation: Authorisation comes before the catalogue and the freebies.

u12l7-9.prompt: The EU regulation governing crypto-asset providers is called ____.
u12l7-9.explanation: Markets in Crypto-Assets. MiFID regulates traditional investment services.

u12l7-10.prompt: Does MiCA protect you from this or not?
options: Losing your seed phrase in self-custody
The platform not disclosing its risks
The exchange mixing your crypto with its own
u12l7-10.explanation: MiCA regulates companies; neither the price nor your own mistakes fall under its protection.
